package.title: Lifecycle — SDVではintegration/diagnostics/validationもArchitectureになる
package.editorial_angle: 中央計算機とサービス分離が進むほど、variant management、CI/CD、自動integration、diagnostics、digital twin/VILがE&E architectureの成立条件になることを示す。
boundaries: The evaluation is a laboratory setup using TurtleBots, ESP32-based ECU emulation and a central backend, not a production vehicle/fleet validation.
The authors explicitly identify deployment to a larger connected-vehicle testbed and deeper feature-model/variant-management integration as future work.
The evaluation uses CARLA and workstation-class hardware to emulate the vehicle/sensor-actuator environment; it does not establish behavior on production automotive compute or physical vehicle buses.

The authors list stronger cybersecurity measures, throughput/processing optimization and reliable real-time operation as future work, so those properties are not fully established by the current evaluation.
The demonstration is a simulated SDV environment; the authors explicitly identify a more comprehensive demonstration with realistic automotive hardware and software as future work.

The authors note that online integration on the vehicle may be restricted to relatively small problems because vehicle compute resources are limited; larger-scale analysis is better suited to design time.
The PoC predefines VMs because the selected ACRN setup has limited runtime configuration flexibility.
Inspect the full paper for dynamometer/vehicle/server setup, synchronization architecture, case-study metrics, and comparison with conventional ViL/HIL.

The accessible primary text does not expose case-study scenario definitions, central-server hardware, timing/accuracy metrics, synchronization error, comparison baseline, or quantitative development-effort reduction.
The evaluation is centered on autonomous-driving software; conclusions about other centralized vehicle domains require separate evidence.
The evaluation is a controlled 5G test-fleet/smart-charging scenario with injected faults rather than broad production-fleet fault distributions.
Graph-based rankings identify likely root causes; their correctness depends on dependency/causal graph quality, anomaly detection, and the selected analysis module.

artifact.canonical_name: An OpenSource CI/CD Pipeline for Variant-Rich Software-Defined Vehicles

sources.title: An OpenSource CI/CD Pipeline for Variant-Rich Software-Defined Vehicles
sources.role: Author arXiv paper/preprint used to verify the architecture, evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The proposed open-source pipeline structures SDV software into development, build/test, artifact storage and deployment stages, with variant metadata driving target-specific artifacts across ECUs, HPCs and backend systems.
A cloud/client OTA middleware pair selects compatible versions from artifact metadata, delivers updates to heterogeneous targets, verifies them and supports rollback/telemetry.

The laboratory evaluation demonstrates variant-specific firmware updates/rollback on emulated ECUs, Snap-based vehicle-control updates, and containerized AI-model deployment to TurtleBot/ROS 2 targets with a backend.

metrics.name: TurtleBots used in AI evaluation
metrics.context: One designated as the Ego TurtleBot for model deployment.

metrics.name: embedded-software vehicle variants evaluated
metrics.context: Variant-specific OTA packages and rollback were tested on two ECU configurations.

limitations.text: The evaluation is a laboratory setup using TurtleBots, ESP32-based ECU emulation and a central backend, not a production vehicle/fleet validation.
The authors explicitly identify deployment to a larger connected-vehicle testbed and deeper feature-model/variant-management integration as future work.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for An OpenSource CI/CD Pipeline for Variant-Rich Software-Defined Vehicles; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The full primary text verifies the variant-aware CI/CD/OTA architecture, ECU/HPC/backend target model, rollback, two embedded variants, three-TurtleBot AI test, and larger-testbed/variant-management future-work boundary.

editorial.why_now_note: SDV architecture extends beyond runtime ECUs: software provenance, target compatibility, OTA, rollback and variant management become part of the vehicle system architecture.
editorial.rationale: Direct evidence for cloud-to-vehicle software lifecycle architecture, including variant derivation, OTA delivery, rollback and multiple deployment target classes.

artifact.canonical_name: AUTOFRAME — A Software-driven Integration Framework for Automotive Systems
artifact.organization: Technical University of Munich / IIT Mandi

sources.title: AUTOFRAME — A Software-driven Integration Framework for Automotive Systems
sources.role: Author paper/preprint used to verify the reported architecture, method/evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: AUTOFRAME centralizes vehicle functions behind a hardware-abstraction layer, standardized module interfaces, connection handling and a deployment handler that uses containers for module isolation and dynamic deployment.
The hardware-abstraction layer derives sensor/actuator adapters from vehicle configuration so application modules can consume standardized data independent of concrete hardware setups.

The authors evaluate the framework in a CARLA-based setup with a separate central-car computer running lane detection, motion planning and control, and demonstrate automated addition of a trajectory-visualization module.
claims.context: Simulation-based evaluation, not an on-road production deployment.

metrics.name: central car computer RAM
metrics.context: Evaluation hardware stated in Table I.

limitations.text: The evaluation uses CARLA and workstation-class hardware to emulate the vehicle/sensor-actuator environment; it does not establish behavior on production automotive compute or physical vehicle buses.

The authors list stronger cybersecurity measures, throughput/processing optimization and reliable real-time operation as future work, so those properties are not fully established by the current evaluation.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for AUTOFRAME -- A Software-driven Integration Framework for Automotive Systems; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The full primary text verifies AUTOFRAME's hardware-abstraction/module/deployment architecture, its CARLA-based two-computer evaluation and dynamic module integration, plus explicit future-work boundaries.

editorial.why_now_note: AUTOFRAME directly illustrates software/hardware decoupling and dynamic deployment as architectural mechanisms for centralized SDV compute.
editorial.rationale: Useful implementation/framework evidence, with simulation and unfinished security/real-time properties kept explicit.

artifact.canonical_name: Automatic Platform Configuration and Software Integration for Software-Defined Vehicles
artifact.organization: Technical University of Munich / University of Bamberg

sources.title: Automatic Platform Configuration and Software Integration for Software-Defined Vehicles
sources.role: Author paper/preprint used to verify the reported architecture, method/evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The authors move platform configuration and software integration toward runtime using an integration manager that combines model-based design-space exploration, code generation, hypervisor partitions, containers, orchestration, and a REST interface.
claims.context: Proposed architecture and implemented proof of concept.

claims.text: The proof-of-concept architecture uses ACRN VMs to separate execution environments and containers within user VMs for application deployment, with predefined constraints used to verify and optimize integration plans.
claims.context: Implemented PoC architecture; this is not evidence of a certified freedom-from-interference argument.

claims.text: The PoC uses an Intel Whiskey Lake board with a Service VM and two User VMs and demonstrates a two-step online integration scenario that adds applications while preserving an existing deployment.

metrics.name: PoC central-computer CPU cores
metrics.context: Whiskey Lake board stated by the authors.

metrics.name: PoC example applications
metrics.context: Selected from OpenVINO, ROS and benchmark tools.

limitations.text: The demonstration is a simulated SDV environment; the authors explicitly identify a more comprehensive demonstration with realistic automotive hardware and software as future work.

The authors note that online integration on the vehicle may be restricted to relatively small problems because vehicle compute resources are limited; larger-scale analysis is better suited to design time.
The PoC predefines VMs because the selected ACRN setup has limited runtime configuration flexibility.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for Automatic Platform Configuration and Software Integration for Software-Defined Vehicles; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The full primary text verifies the integration-manager architecture, ACRN/K3S/Terraform-based PoC, two-step runtime integration flow, hardware setup, and explicit realism/scale limitations.

editorial.why_now_note: The work directly relocates software-to-hardware allocation and integration from a design-time-only responsibility toward an orchestrated runtime responsibility on centralized compute.
editorial.rationale: Strong evidence for the development/runtime boundary shift in SDV architecture, provided the simulated-PoC limitation is retained.

artifact.canonical_name: From Code to Road: A Vehicle-in-the-Loop and Digital Twin-Based Framework for Central Car Server Testing in Autonomous Driving

sources.title: From Code to Road: A Vehicle-in-the-Loop and Digital Twin-Based Framework for Central Car Server Testing in Autonomous Driving
sources.role: Author arXiv paper/preprint used to verify the architecture, evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The proposed test framework couples a physical vehicle on a dynamometer with a synchronized digital twin to validate software on a centralized E/E architecture.

The framework runs the full autonomous-driving software directly on central-car-server vehicle hardware after simulation, avoiding separate physical-ECU/protocol testing and intermediate reflashing layers.
The authors report experimental case studies across multiple scenarios and argue that mixed virtual/physical testing can reduce early full-hardware integration effort.

limitations.text: The accessible primary text does not expose case-study scenario definitions, central-server hardware, timing/accuracy metrics, synchronization error, comparison baseline, or quantitative development-effort reduction.
The evaluation is centered on autonomous-driving software; conclusions about other centralized vehicle domains require separate evidence.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for From Code to Road: A Vehicle-in-the-Loop and Digital Twin-Based Framework for Central Car Server Testing in Autonomous Driving; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The primary abstract verifies the physical-vehicle/digital-twin coupling, central-car-server execution model and experimental-case-study claim, but detailed setup and quantitative outcomes remain unresolved.

unresolved_questions: Inspect the full paper for dynamometer/vehicle/server setup, synchronization architecture, case-study metrics, and comparison with conventional ViL/HIL.

editorial.why_now_note: Central-server consolidation changes validation architecture: testing moves from many ECU/protocol units toward whole-software-stack hardware-in-loop/digital-twin workflows.
editorial.rationale: Architecture-significant lifecycle evidence even though detailed experimental metrics remain unresolved; include qualitatively with an explicit evidence-depth caveat.

artifact.canonical_name: SDVDiag: A Modular Platform for the Diagnosis of Connected Vehicle Functions

sources.title: SDVDiag: A Modular Platform for the Diagnosis of Connected Vehicle Functions
sources.role: Author arXiv paper/preprint used to verify the architecture, evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: SDVDiag is a modular diagnosis platform that builds continuously updated dependency/causal graphs from distributed observability data, snapshots them around incidents, and ranks likely root causes.
The platform supports interchangeable runtime modules for graph processing, anomaly detection and incident analysis, allowing the diagnosis pipeline to adapt to system behavior.
The authors deploy SDVDiag in a University of Stuttgart 5G connected-vehicle test-fleet environment and report reliable detection of injected faults in a smart-charging/distributed-function scenario.
claims.context: Test-fleet result, not a fleet-wide production validation.

limitations.text: The evaluation is a controlled 5G test-fleet/smart-charging scenario with injected faults rather than broad production-fleet fault distributions.
Graph-based rankings identify likely root causes; their correctness depends on dependency/causal graph quality, anomaly detection, and the selected analysis module.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for SDVDiag: A Modular Platform for the Diagnosis of Connected Vehicle Functions; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The full primary text verifies the modular data/graph/anomaly/root-cause pipeline, runtime module exchange, 5G test-fleet deployment and injected-fault evaluation; its controlled-scenario boundary remains explicit.

editorial.why_now_note: Cloud/edge/in-vehicle functional chains make diagnostics an architecture-wide observability problem, expanding the lifecycle responsibility beyond ECU-local UDS/OBD-style diagnostics.
editorial.rationale: Useful lifecycle/operations evidence showing that distributed vehicle-edge-cloud dependencies require graph-based observability and root-cause analysis beyond traditional ECU diagnostics.
